If a book comes back late, many libraries charge a small overdue fine,
though a growing number have stopped charging fines for ordinary
lateness and instead bill only for lost or damaged items. Most systems
also send reminders by email or text before and after the due date. If
a book is truly lost, the borrower typically pays the replacement cost,
sometimes plus a processing fee, and the record is cleared once the
account is settled.

Behind the scenes, the library keeps track of every item so the
collection stays in order and remains available to everyone. That
shared responsibility is what makes public lending work: you get free
access to books, and the library gets them back for the next reader.
